problems.title: Two Sum
problems.summary: Given an integer array and a target, find two different positions whose values add to that target. Return the original indices of the two values, in either order. Assume exactly one valid pair exists, and do not use the same array element twice.

examples.explanation: The values 5 and 8 add to 13 and are at indices 2 and 3.
The values 3 and 10 add to 13.

thinking.insight: For a value x, its partner must be target - x. A hash map checks whether that partner appeared earlier without scanning the array again.
steps: Create a map from earlier values to indices.
For each index i, calculate need = target - nums[i].
If need is in the map, return its saved index and i.
Otherwise store the current value and index.

bruteForce.description: Check every pair of different positions.
steps: Choose each first index i.
Try every later index j.
Return the pair when the sum equals target.

optimal.description: Use a hash map for expected constant-time complement lookups.
steps: Visit each value once.
Compute its complement.
Check the map before insertion.
Return both indices when found.

python.code:
def twoSum(nums, target):
    seen = {}  # Map earlier values to their indices.
    for i, num in enumerate(nums):  # Visit each position once.
        need = target - num  # Find the required complement.
        if need in seen:  # Check only earlier positions.
            return [seen[need], i]  # Return original indices.
        seen[num] = i  # Insert after checking to avoid reusing this index.
    return []  # Defensive fallback; a pair is guaranteed.

mistakes: Returning values instead of indices.
Inserting before checking can reuse the same position.
Sorting without preserving original indices.
edgeCases: The pair occurs at the end.

hints.hint1: Can you avoid checking every pair?
hints.hint2: Calculate target minus the current value.
hints.hint3: Store earlier values in a hash map and check the complement before insertion.

problems.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problems.summary: Given a string, find the length of its longest contiguous substring in which every character appears at most once. The substring must preserve the original character order. Return its length rather than the substring itself.

examples.explanation: The substring "bcaef" contains no repeated characters and has length 5.
Any valid substring can contain only one of the repeated characters.

constraints: s may contain English letters, digits, symbols, and spaces.

Move the right boundary across the string.
If the current character was last seen inside the window, move the left boundary forward.
Record the current character's index.
Update the maximum window length.

steps: Choose each starting index.
Extend the ending index.
Check whether the substring contains duplicates and update the best length.
bruteForce.time: O(n^3) with substring creation and duplicate checks

optimal.description: Use a sliding window and last-seen indices so each character is processed once.
steps: Track the left edge of the valid window.
Use a map to locate each character's last position.
Jump the left edge forward only when the repeated character is inside the current window.
Update the best window length.

python.code:
def lengthOfLongestSubstring(s):
    last = {}  # Character -> most recent index.
    left = 0  # Left edge of the current duplicate-free window.
    best = 0  # Longest valid window found so far.
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):  # Extend the window one character at a time.
        if ch in last and last[ch] >= left:  # Repeat is inside the current window.
            left = last[ch] + 1  # Move left edge beyond the earlier occurrence.
        last[ch] = right  # Record the current occurrence.
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)  # Update valid window length.
    return best  # Return the maximum length.

mistakes: Moving the left edge backward when a character's old occurrence is outside the current window.
Using right - left instead of right - left + 1.
Clearing the entire map each time a duplicate appears.
edgeCases: All characters are identical, so the answer is 1 for non-empty input.
A repeated character appears before the current window's left edge.

hints.hint1: What makes a substring valid here?
hints.hint2: Track the most recent index of each character.
hints.hint3: If its last index is at least the current left boundary, move left to last_index + 1.

problems.title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
problems.summary: Given two sorted arrays, find the median of their combined sorted values in O(log(m+n)) time. Rather than merging every element, binary-search a partition in the shorter array so the left partitions contain half the total elements and all left values are no greater than all right values. For example, [1,3] and [2] have median 2. The arrays [1,2] and [3,4] have median 2.5.

examples.explanation: The merged order would be [1,2,3], whose middle value is 2.
The two middle values are 2 and 3, so their average is 2.5.

constraints: nums1 and nums2 are sorted in non-decreasing order.
The required time complexity is O(log(m+n)).

howToThink.insight: Choose cuts in both arrays so the left side has half the elements. A correct partition has max(left side) <= min(right side); search only the cut in the shorter array.
steps: Swap arrays if needed so nums1 is shorter.
Binary-search a cut i in nums1 and derive j = (m+n+1)//2 - i.
Use boundary sentinels when a cut is at an array edge.
If left values cross, move the cut; when the partition is valid, return the middle boundary value or average of the two middle boundaries.

bruteForce.idea: Merge the two sorted arrays, then read the middle one or two values.

optimal.idea: Binary-search the partition in the shorter array and use partition boundary values to calculate the median.

solutions.python:
class Solution:
    def findMedianSortedArrays(self, nums1: list[int], nums2: list[int]) -> float:
        # Binary-search the shorter array to minimize iterations.
        if len(nums1) > len(nums2):
            nums1, nums2 = nums2, nums1
        m, n = len(nums1), len(nums2)
        left_size = (m + n + 1) // 2
        left, right = 0, m
        while left <= right:
            i = left + (right - left) // 2  # Cut in the shorter array.
            j = left_size - i  # Matching cut in the other array.
            a_left = float("-inf") if i == 0 else nums1[i - 1]
            a_right = float("inf") if i == m else nums1[i]
            b_left = float("-inf") if j == 0 else nums2[j - 1]
            b_right = float("inf") if j == n else nums2[j]
            if a_left <= b_right and b_left <= a_right:  # Valid partition.
                if (m + n) % 2:  # Odd count: left side has the median.
                    return float(max(a_left, b_left))
                # Even count: average the largest left and smallest right.
                return (max(a_left, b_left) + min(a_right, b_right)) / 2.0
            if a_left > b_right:  # Too many nums1 values on the left.
                right = i - 1
            else:  # Too few nums1 values on the left.
                left = i + 1
        raise ValueError("Input arrays must be sorted")

commonMistakes: Binary-searching the longer array, which can make a partition index invalid.
Using the wrong partition size for odd totals.
Forgetting empty-array boundaries or using ordinary array indices at edges.
Adding two int values before casting to double in Java or C++.
edgeCases: All values in one array are smaller than all values in the other.
Combined length is odd or even.
Negative values and repeated values across the arrays.
hints: You only need the values immediately around a correct partition, not a merged array.
Make the shorter array the one you binary-search; the other cut is determined by the desired left-side size.
A valid partition satisfies max(left values) <= min(right values); use negative and positive infinity at missing boundaries.

problems.title: Longest Palindromic Substring
problems.summary: Given a string, return one of its longest contiguous substrings that reads the same forward and backward. If several answers have the same maximum length, any one of them is acceptable. A palindrome can have either one central character or a central gap between two characters.

examples.explanation: The first five characters form a palindrome.
The final two characters form the longest palindrome in this string.

thinking.insight: Every palindrome has a center. Try each character as an odd-length center and each gap as an even-length center, expanding outward while the two characters match.
steps: Remember the start and length of the best palindrome.
For every index, expand around that single-character center.
Also expand around the gap between that index and the next.
Stop an expansion when characters differ or a boundary is crossed.
Update the best range whenever a longer palindrome is found.

bruteForce.description: Check all substrings and test whether each reads identically in reverse.
steps: Enumerate each start and end index.
Compare characters from both ends inward.
Remember the longest substring that passes the palindrome check.

optimal.description: Expand from every odd and even center.
steps: For each center, initialize left and right pointers.
Expand while both pointers remain in bounds and characters match.
Record the longest range across all centers.

python.code:
def longestPalindrome(s):
    best_start, best_len = 0, 1  # Any single character is a palindrome.
    def expand(left, right):  # Return the inclusive range of a centered palindrome.
        while left >= 0 and right < len(s) and s[left] == s[right]:  # Keep matching pairs.
            left -= 1  # Expand one position to the left.
            right += 1  # Expand one position to the right.
        return left + 1, right - left - 1  # Convert failed boundary to valid range.
    for center in range(len(s)):  # Try every character as a center.
        for left, right in (expand(center, center), expand(center, center + 1)):  # Odd and even centers.
            if right > best_len:  # Keep only a longer palindrome.
                best_start, best_len = left, right
    return s[best_start:best_start + best_len]  # Return the best substring.

mistakes: Only checking odd-length palindromes and missing even-length answers such as "cc".
Reading outside the string bounds before comparing characters.
Returning an end index as if it were a length.
edgeCases: The longest palindrome has even length.
Several palindromes tie for maximum length.

hints.hint1: A palindrome mirrors around a center.
hints.hint2: Try both a character center and a gap center.
hints.hint3: Expand two pointers outward while characters match, tracking the longest valid range.

problems.title: Longest Common Prefix
problems.summary: Given a list of strings, return the longest prefix shared by every string. A prefix must begin at the first character of each string. If the strings have no common starting character, return an empty string.

examples.explanation: All three strings start with "inte", but their next characters differ.
The strings do not share a first character.

constraints: strs[i] contains lowercase English letters when non-empty.

thinking.insight: The common prefix cannot be longer than the shortest string. Compare characters by position across all strings and stop at the first mismatch.
steps: If any string is empty, the answer is empty.
Use the first string as a candidate prefix.
For each character position, compare that character in every string.
Stop at a mismatch or when the first string ends.
Return the matching prefix.

bruteForce.description: Compare every candidate prefix length against every string.
steps: Try prefix lengths from one upward.
Check whether every string begins with the candidate prefix.
Stop when a candidate fails.
bruteForce.time: O(S) for total compared characters with direct checks

At each position, compare every other string's character.
Stop on mismatch or a string boundary.
Return the prefix before that position.

python.code:
def longestCommonPrefix(strs):
    if not strs:  # Defensive handling for an empty list.
        return ""
    first = strs[0]  # Use the first string as the reference.
    for i, ch in enumerate(first):  # Test each possible prefix position.
        for other in strs[1:]:  # Compare against every remaining string.
            if i >= len(other) or other[i] != ch:  # Stop at boundary or mismatch.
                return first[:i]  # Everything before i is shared.
    return first  # The entire first string is a shared prefix.

mistakes: Checking only the first and last strings without justification.
Accessing a character after a shorter string has ended.
Confusing a common substring with a common prefix.
edgeCases: The strings have no shared first character.

hints.hint1: A prefix always begins at index zero.
hints.hint2: The answer cannot be longer than the first string.
hints.hint3: Compare each character position across every string and stop at the first mismatch.

problems.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
problems.summary: Given a linked list, remove its nth node from the end and return the head. The goal is to do this in one pass using two pointers separated by n nodes. For example, [1,2,3,4,5] with n = 2 becomes [1,2,3,5]. A dummy node makes removing the original head straightforward.

examples.explanation: The second node from the end, with value 4, is removed.
The only node is removed.

constraints: The number of nodes in the list is sz.

howToThink.insight: Keep fast n nodes ahead of slow. When fast reaches the last node, slow is positioned just before the node to remove.
steps: Create a dummy node pointing to head; start slow and fast at dummy.
Advance fast n steps.
Move both pointers until fast.next is null.
Skip the target node with slow.next = slow.next.next.
Return dummy.next.

bruteForce.idea: Count the list length, then walk to the node immediately before the target and unlink it.

optimal.idea: Use a dummy node and a fixed n-node gap between fast and slow pointers in one traversal.

solutions.python:
class Solution:
    def removeNthFromEnd(self, head, n: int):
        dummy = ListNode(0, head)  # Handles removal of the original head.
        slow = fast = dummy
        for _ in range(n):  # Create an n-node gap.
            fast = fast.next
        while fast.next:  # Stop with fast at the final node.
            slow = slow.next
            fast = fast.next
        slow.next = slow.next.next  # Bypass the target node.
        return dummy.next

commonMistakes: Not using a dummy node, making head deletion a special case.
Moving fast one step too few or too many.
Trying to access fast.next after it is null.
edgeCases: Remove the head (n equals list length).
hints: The node to delete needs its previous node, so stop slow one node before the target.
A dummy node gives the head a predecessor.
Advance fast n steps first, then move both pointers until fast is at the last node.

problems.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
problems.summary: Given the heads of two sorted linked lists, merge them into one sorted linked list by reusing the existing nodes. Return the merged list's head. For example, [1,2,4] and [1,3,4] merge into [1,1,2,3,4,4]. If one list runs out first, attach the rest of the other list.

examples.explanation: Choose the smaller current node from the two lists at each step.
The non-empty list is already the answer.

constraints: The number of nodes in both lists is in the range [0, 50].
Both list1 and list2 are sorted in non-decreasing order.

howToThink.insight: The smallest remaining value must be at one of the two list heads, so repeatedly attach the smaller head to a result list.
steps: Create a dummy node and let tail point to it.
Compare list1.val and list2.val; attach the smaller node and advance that list.
Advance tail after every attachment.
When either list ends, attach the other list's remainder and return dummy.next.

bruteForce.idea: Collect values from both lists, sort them, and build a new list.

optimal.idea: Merge by comparing current heads and relinking existing nodes; append the remaining suffix at the end.

solutions.python:
class Solution:
    def mergeTwoLists(self, list1, list2):
        dummy = ListNode(0)  # Sentinel simplifies handling the result head.
        tail = dummy
        while list1 and list2:
            if list1.val <= list2.val:  # Take the smaller current node.
                tail.next = list1
                list1 = list1.next
            else:
                tail.next = list2
                list2 = list2.next
            tail = tail.next  # Advance the result tail.
        tail.next = list1 if list1 else list2  # Attach remaining nodes.
        return dummy.next

commonMistakes: Forgetting to advance the pointer of the list whose node was attached.
Creating a cycle by linking the tail incorrectly.
Building a new list unnecessarily when existing nodes can be reused.
edgeCases: Values are equal at both heads.
One list is entirely smaller than the other.
hints: At every step, only compare the two nodes currently at the front.
A dummy head makes the first attachment no different from later attachments.
Once one list is empty, the other list is already sorted and can be attached directly.

problems.title: First Missing Positive
problems.summary: Given an unsorted integer array, return the smallest positive integer that does not occur in it. Values may be negative, zero, repeated, or much larger than the array length. Aim for linear time and constant auxiliary space by placing useful values into their natural index positions.

examples.explanation: The positive integers 1, 3, and 4 occur, while 2 is absent.
Both 1 and 2 occur, so the smallest missing positive is 3.

thinking.insight: For an array of length n, the answer is at most n + 1. A value v in the range 1..n belongs at index v - 1. Place values in-place, while preventing duplicate values from causing endless swaps.
steps: Let n be the array length.
While a value v is in 1..n and not already at index v - 1, swap it into that destination.
Scan from left to right.
The first index i where nums[i] differs from i + 1 gives answer i + 1.
If all slots match, return n + 1.

bruteForce.description: Test positive candidates one by one by searching the full array for each candidate.
steps: Start candidate at 1.
Search the array for it.
Return it if absent; otherwise increment and repeat.

optimal.description: Use in-place cyclic placement to move each relevant positive integer to its natural index.
steps: Ignore values outside 1..n.
Swap each in-range value toward index value - 1.
Skip swapping if the destination already holds that value.
Return the first index whose value is not index + 1.

python.code:
def firstMissingPositive(nums):
    n = len(nums)  # The answer cannot exceed n + 1.
    for i in range(n):  # Place useful values into their home indices.
        while 1 <= nums[i] <= n and nums[nums[i] - 1] != nums[i]:  # Guard range and duplicates.
            target = nums[i] - 1  # Value v belongs at index v - 1.
            nums[i], nums[target] = nums[target], nums[i]  # Swap value into its home slot.
    for i, value in enumerate(nums):  # Inspect the rearranged array.
        if value != i + 1:  # The expected value for this slot is missing.
            return i + 1  # Return the first missing positive.
    return n + 1  # All values 1 through n are present.

class Solution:
    def permute(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
        result, path = [], []
        used = [False] * len(nums)
        def dfs():
            if len(path) == len(nums):
                result.append(path.copy())
                return
            for i, value in enumerate(nums):
                if used[i]: continue
                used[i] = True
                path.append(value)
                dfs()
                path.pop()
                used[i] = False
        dfs()
        return result

from collections import deque

class Solution:
    def levelOrder(self, root) -> list[list[int]]:
        if root is None:  # No nodes means no levels.
            return []
        queue = deque([root])  # FIFO queue starts with the root.
        result = []
        while queue:
            level_size = len(queue)  # Freeze this level's node count.
            level = []
            for _ in range(level_size):  # Process only current-level nodes.
                node = queue.popleft()
                level.append(node.val)
                if node.left:
                    queue.append(node.left)  # Children belong to next level.
                if node.right:
                    queue.append(node.right)
            result.append(level)
        return result

commonMistakes: Using the queue's changing size as the loop condition for the current level.
Pushing null children into the queue.
Using a stack when level-order traversal requires FIFO order.

def isPalindrome(s):
    left, right = 0, len(s) - 1  # Start at opposite ends.
    while left < right:  # Stop when pointers meet or cross.
        while left < right and not s[left].isalnum():  # Ignore punctuation and spaces.
            left += 1  # Move toward the center.
        while left < right and not s[right].isalnum():  # Ignore from the right too.
            right -= 1  # Move toward the center.
        if s[left].lower() != s[right].lower():  # Compare case-insensitively.
            return False  # A mismatch disproves the palindrome.
        left += 1  # Consume the matching left character.
        right -= 1  # Consume the matching right character.
    return True  # Every compared pair matched.

        if not head or not head.next:
            return
        slow, fast = head, head  # Find the midpoint.
        while fast.next and fast.next.next:
            slow = slow.next
            fast = fast.next.next
        second = slow.next  # Start of the second half.
        slow.next = None  # Split the list into two lists.
        previous = None
        while second:  # Reverse the second half.
            next_node = second.next
            second.next = previous
            previous = second
            second = next_node
        first, second = head, previous

            first.next = second
            second.next = first_next
            first, second = first_next, second_next

Find the next required character.
Fail if it does not exist; otherwise continue.

Visit each character of t once.
Advance i on a match.

def isSubsequence(s, t):
    i = 0  # Index of the next character needed from s.
    for ch in t:  # Scan the candidate string once.
        if i < len(s) and s[i] == ch:  # This character matches the next requirement.
            i += 1  # Advance to the next required character.
        if i == len(s):  # Every character in s has been matched.
            return True
    return i == len(s)  # The empty s is also a subsequence.

Advancing the s pointer on a non-match.
Forgetting the empty string is a subsequence of every string.

hints.hint2: Keep a pointer to the next character needed from s.

steps: Set left and right to the first and last valid indices.
Compute the middle index and compare nums[mid] with target.
If equal, return mid; if smaller, move left past mid; otherwise move right before mid.

optimal.idea: Use a shrinking inclusive search interval and discard half after each comparison.

solutions.python:
class Solution:
    def search(self, nums: list[int], target: int) -> int:
        left, right = 0, len(nums) - 1  # Search the full array.
        while left <= right:  # Continue while the interval is valid.
            mid = left + (right - left) // 2  # Avoid overflow in fixed-width languages.
            if nums[mid] == target:  # Found the target.
                return mid
            if nums[mid] < target:  # Target can only be to the right.
                left = mid + 1
            else:  # Target can only be to the left.
                right = mid - 1
        return -1  # No matching value exists.

commonMistakes: Using left < right with an inclusive interval and accidentally skipping a candidate.
Updating left = mid or right = mid - 1 inconsistently, which can cause an infinite loop.
Applying binary search to an unsorted array.

Target is smaller than every value or larger than every value.
hints: What property lets you rule out half the array after one comparison?

problems.title: Last Stone Weight
problems.summary: Repeatedly smash the two heaviest stones. Equal stones both disappear; otherwise the difference becomes a new stone. Return the last stone's weight or zero if none remain. A max-heap efficiently exposes the two heaviest stones each round.

examples.explanation: Repeatedly smash the two heaviest stones.

constraints: Inputs follow the problem's stated format and bounds; see the linked LeetCode statement for the full limits.

howToThink.insight: Use a max-heap because each operation needs the two largest remaining values.
steps: Build a max-heap from all stones.
Remove the two largest stones.
If their weights differ, insert the difference.
Continue until at most one stone remains.

bruteForce.idea: Sort the list every round and take the two largest.

optimal.idea: Use a max-heap for repeated largest-element extraction.

commonMistakes: Using a min-heap and extracting the lightest stones.
Reinserting a zero-weight stone when the two weights match.
Forgetting the case where all stones disappear.
hints: Each round asks for the two maximum values.
A max-heap gives both values efficiently.
Only reinsert the positive difference when the weights differ.

problems.title: Longest Common Subsequence
problems.summary: Given two strings, return the length of their longest common subsequence. Characters must appear in the same relative order in both strings, but they do not need to be adjacent. For text1 = "abcde" and text2 = "ace", the answer is 3 because "ace" appears in both in order. If the current characters match, extend the result for the prefixes before them; otherwise take the better result from skipping one character in either string.

examples.explanation: The longest common subsequence is "ace".
All characters match in order.
There are no shared characters.

constraints: text1 and text2 consist of lowercase English characters.

howToThink.insight: Let dp[i][j] be the LCS length for the first i characters of text1 and first j characters of text2.
steps: Initialize row 0 and column 0 to zero because an empty string has no common subsequence.
If the next characters match, use 1 + dp[i-1][j-1].
If they differ, take max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
Return the state for the full lengths.

bruteForce.idea: Recursively explore matching or skipping characters without caching overlapping states.

optimal.idea: Fill a two-dimensional DP table for all prefix pairs.

commonMistakes: Confusing subsequence with substring, which must be contiguous.
Using dp[i-1][j-1] alone when characters differ.
Forgetting the extra row and column for empty prefixes or mixing 0-based and 1-based indices.
edgeCases: One string is a subsequence of the other.
Repeated characters appear in both strings.
hints: Define a state for prefixes of both strings.
When characters match, you can append that character to the best result for the shorter prefixes.
When they differ, compare the result from skipping the last character of either string.
